title: Results and diagnosis
summary: A test is only useful if its result reaches someone. For a production go/no-go decision one bit per memory is enough; for repair and for yield learning the chip must also say **where** it failed. This topic follows a fail from the comparator to the tester.
objectives: Explain sticky fail flags and the go/no-go result.
Describe diagnosis modes: fail capture, stop and resume, bitmaps.
Explain why ROMs are checked with a signature.

steps.title: Comparator
steps.md: Every read is compared bit by bit with the expected data.

steps.title: Sticky fail flag
steps.md: A mismatch sets a **fail flag** that stays set until the next test — it is *sticky*. At the end, *pass = not fail*. This is the **go / no-go** result.

steps.title: Diagnosis register
steps.md: In diagnosis mode the controller also captures **where**: the element, the address and which bits were wrong.

steps.title: Read out
steps.md: The record is shifted out through TAP/IJTAG. To log more fails, the test **stops** at a fail, the record is read, and the test **resumes** — again and again.

rows: **Go / no-go**

**Per-bit fail**

blocks.caption: How much the chip remembers about its fails

blocks.title: Why not always keep everything?
blocks.md: Every fail record costs **register area** and **read-out time** through the slow JTAG port. Production wants a fast decision; detailed diagnosis is only switched on for chips being analysed or repaired.
Plot every failing cell at its **physical** row and column (using the scrambling information) and you get a **failure bitmap**. Its shape points to the defect:

rows: single cell
defect inside one cell: a weak transistor, a particle
two adjacent cells
a bridge between neighbours — a coupling fault
a whole row
broken word line or row decoder defect
a whole column
broken bit line, sense amplifier or column mux
a cluster of cells
a large particle or a local process problem
the same cells on many chips
a design or layout weakness, not a random defect
blocks.caption: Reading a failure bitmap

blocks.prompt: Practice: what is the most likely cause?

blocks.md:
A ROM cannot be written, so the controller cannot know the expected data at each address — unless it stored a copy of the ROM, which would make no sense. Instead MBIST **reads every address** and compacts the data in a **MISR**, exactly as in *BIST Foundations*:

> {⇑(r); ⇓(r)} → MISR → compare with the golden signature

The golden signature is computed from the ROM content when the chip is designed. Reading in both directions also catches address-decoder faults.

blocks.caption: ROM test: address counter, ROM, MISR and one compare at the end

blocks.title: Compare or compact?
blocks.md: **Compare** when the expected data is known (RAM: the test wrote it). **Compact** when it is not (ROM, or logic). Compacting gives only pass/fail — it cannot say *which* address failed.

It is cleared after every correct read.
It counts the number of fails.
It stops the memory clock.

questions.text: Why does production usually run in go/no-go mode?
options: It is fastest and needs the least read-out through the slow JTAG port.
Diagnosis mode cannot run at speed.
Go/no-go finds more faults.
Production chips have no diagnosis registers.

A single weak cell
